newsitem.title: USA: Low U.S. jobless claims more than a fluke-experts.
newsitem.headline: Low U.S. jobless claims more than a fluke-experts.

text.p: Claims for unemployment benefits in the United States held below 320,000 for the fifth week in a row last week, adding to concerns about labor market tightness, analysts said.

"The labor markets are tight and they are getting tighter," said John Park, an economist at Sanwa Securities (USA) Co. "The mystery is why it's not showing through into higher wages and higher price levels."

Weekly jobless claims fell to 307,000 in the week ended March 8 from a revised 312,000 the week before, the Labor Department reported on Thursday. The four-week moving average declined to 310,250 from a revised 310,500.
Economists in a Reuters poll had projected a weekly claims total of 313,000.
The decline in the four-week claims average was of particular interest to analysts. For the first few weeks of its slide, economists attributed much of the dip to seasonal-adjustment quirks.
But seasonals alone can no longer explain the persisting trend, analysts said.
"You can blame seasonal factors on a week-to-week basis, but I don't think you can blame seasonal factors for a month," said Dan Seto, senior economist at Nikko Secruties Co International Inc.
"We've been at these levels for five weeks now with few exceptions," he added.
That suggests a strong payrolls component in the March employment report, even though the week ended March 8 was officially part of the February survey period, Seto said.

Coupled with an exceptionally strong upward revision to January retail sales, the jobless claims data could put additional pressure on the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates in order to head off inflation, some analysts said.
Sanwa's Park said the benign inflation data expected over the next week may not be enough to stay the Fed's hand.
"In spite of what the (consumer and producer price) data might tell us, if (central bankers) want to do the preemptive move, they definitely have cover to do that," Park said.
Retail sales for January were reported up a revised 1.5 percent, and February sales grew 0.8 percent.
"The whole key to the economy is the consumer, and the consumer doesn't want to stop shopping," said Park, echoing comments made recently by Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan.
